account: Thames Water trialed Origin Orbit, the satellite leak-detection product of North East England start-up Origin Tech Ltd (founded 2019). The company and the utility describe it as applying artificial intelligence to satellite data to flag suspected underground leaks within a 30-meter search radius. In August 2025 The Times reported that Northumbrian Water technicians used Origin's satellite points to narrow leak searches to a 20-meter radius. The company's founding director told the paper that its leak totals came mainly from trials. Thames Water's statements say that an 18-week trial found over 800 leaks across the network, saving an estimated 8.7 million liters of water a day, with several leaks running at more than 10 liters per second. No source dates the Thames Water trial. On the strength of the trial, Thames Water signed a 13-month contract, launched in March 2026 according to the utility's release. It deploys 20 specialists, with leak-detection crews expected to find about 25 leaks a week each, and aims to cut leakage by 100 million liters a day. That makes Thames Water the first water company to integrate Origin Orbit into business-as-usual leakage operations. Smart Water Magazine reported the result on 5 May 2026. The BBC reported the utility's figures on 20 May 2026, and trade press reproduced them. Origin's co-founder John Marsden told the BBC that the satellites pass over Swindon roughly every six days. He said that they produce points on a map for Thames Water crews. Origin Tech's own site adds a 2026 claim that Origin Orbit identified over 5,000 leaks (73.45 megaliters a day) across its customers. In June 2026 the Irish News reported that NI Water had signed a three-year Origin Orbit contract. On 24 August 2026 Thames Water described the satellite detection as part of its drought-response leak hunting, without reporting leak counts after the trial. New Civil Engineer (25 August 2026) gives the trial's length as 19 weeks, against 18 weeks in the utility's release. All figures originate with the utility and the vendor, and no regulator or independent measurement is among the sources. Cambridgeshire County Council's AI inspection contract (April 2026) and Hertfordshire's ARRES robot (January 2024) have no outcomes on record. They are not among the sources.

ai_role.statement: Only the vendor and the utility describe the AI role. The BBC caption says the AI-generated satellite technology detects moisture and movement in the ground, and Origin Tech describes AI-driven satellite insights. The system outputs suspected-leak points that Thames Water crews then locate and repair with conventional methods. The 800-leak and 8.7 million liters a day figures are Thames Water's estimates relayed by the BBC. They are reproduced in the utility's press release (Water Magazine) and trade press. Origin Tech's site adds vendor claims. No independent verification is among the sources.

fields.account: Thames Water trialed Origin Orbit, the satellite leak-detection product of North East England start-up Origin Tech Ltd (founded 2019). The company and the utility describe it as applying artificial intelligence to satellite data to flag suspected underground leaks within a 30-meter search radius. In August 2025 The Times reported that Northumbrian Water technicians used Origin's satellite points to narrow leak searches to a 20-meter radius. The company's founding director told the paper that its leak totals came mainly from trials. Thames Water's statements say that an 18-week trial found over 800 leaks across the network, saving an estimated 8.7 million liters of water a day, with several leaks running at more than 10 liters per second. No source dates the Thames Water trial. On the strength of the trial, Thames Water signed a 13-month contract, launched in March 2026 according to the utility's release. It deploys 20 specialists, with leak-detection crews expected to find about 25 leaks a week each, and aims to cut leakage by 100 million liters a day. That makes Thames Water the first water company to integrate Origin Orbit into business-as-usual leakage operations. Smart Water Magazine reported the result on 5 May 2026. The BBC reported the utility's figures on 20 May 2026, and trade press reproduced them. Origin's co-founder John Marsden told the BBC that the satellites pass over Swindon roughly every six days. He said that they produce points on a map for Thames Water crews. Origin Tech's own site adds a 2026 claim that Origin Orbit identified over 5,000 leaks (73.45 megaliters a day) across its customers. In June 2026 the Irish News reported that NI Water had signed a three-year Origin Orbit contract. On 24 August 2026 Thames Water described the satellite detection as part of its drought-response leak hunting, without reporting leak counts after the trial. New Civil Engineer (25 August 2026) gives the trial's length as 19 weeks, against 18 weeks in the utility's release. All figures originate with the utility and the vendor, and no regulator or independent measurement is among the sources. Cambridgeshire County Council's AI inspection contract (April 2026) and Hertfordshire's ARRES robot (January 2024) have no outcomes on record. They are not among the sources.
